title: Blastomycosis
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Blastomycosis is a dimorphic fungal infection caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, usually acquired by inhalation of soil spores. It presents as a pulmonary disease that can disseminate to skin, bone, genitourinary tract and CNS, especially in immunocompromised hosts.

sections.p: Blastomycosis is a fungal infection endemic to moist soils in North America. It is caused by the dimorphic fungus Blastomyces dermatitidis, which exists as mould in the environment and as a broad‑based budding yeast in human tissue.
b: Dimorphic fungus; mould in soil, yeast in tissue
Inhalation of conidia is the main route
Common in men, but affects all ages

sections.p: The yeast form shows large, thick‑walled cells with broad‑based budding, a pathognomonic feature on histology. The mould produces arthroconidia that are the infectious particles.
Spore‑laden soil disturbed by farming, construction or wood work releases arthroconidia. Inhalation leads to pulmonary infection; the organism can then disseminate.
b: Environmental reservoir: moist soil, decaying wood

sections.p: Primary pulmonary disease ranges from asymptomatic to severe pneumonia or ARDS. Dissemination occurs in up to 50 % of untreated cases, commonly affecting skin, bone, genitourinary tract and CNS.
b: Pulmonary symptoms: cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain
Skin lesions: verrucous plaques or ulcerated nodules
Bone pain, fractures, urinary symptoms, meningitis

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, imaging, and laboratory confirmation. In low‑resource settings, sputum microscopy and culture are essential; serology and antigen tests may be unavailable.

t.b: Detects broad‑based budding yeast; positive result confirms infection
Grows mould; confirms diagnosis but takes 1–3 weeks
Shows broad‑based budding yeast; definitive in disseminated disease
Rapid but may cross‑react with Histoplasma; useful if available

sections.p: First‑line therapy is amphotericin B for severe disease, followed by itraconazole for 6–12 months. In low‑resource settings, amphotericin B may be limited; fluconazole can be used for mild disease but is less effective.
b: Fluconazole – alternative when itraconazole unavailable, but lower efficacy

t.b: Used in severe pulmonary, CNS or bone disease; monitor renal function and electrolytes
Preferred for moderate disease; monitor liver function and drug interactions
Alternative when other azoles unavailable; less effective against blastomycosis

sections.p: Remember the broad‑based budding yeast on histology. In endemic areas, consider blastomycosis in any patient with chronic cough and skin lesions. HIV and TB co‑infection increase risk of dissemination.
b: Chest X‑ray may show cavitation; CT better for bone involvement

whenToSeekHelp: Severe respiratory distress, haemoptysis, neurological signs (headache, seizures), sudden worsening of skin lesions, or any sign of organ failure

faq.q: How is blastomycosis different from histoplasmosis?
faq.a: Both are dimorphic fungi; histoplasma shows narrow‑based budding yeast and is endemic to Ohio/Mississippi valleys, while blastomyces shows broad‑based budding yeast and is found in moist soils across North America.

faq.q: Can blastomycosis be transmitted from person to person?
faq.a: No, it is not contagious; infection occurs from environmental exposure to soil spores.

faq.q: What is the most reliable diagnostic test in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Microscopy of sputum or biopsy showing broad‑based budding yeast is the quickest confirmatory test; culture is definitive but slower.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with chronic cough and a verrucous skin nodule – what is the most likely diagnosis? — Broad‑based budding yeast on biopsy confirms blastomycosis; consider differential of squamous cell carcinoma.
A patient with HIV develops fever, cough and new bone pain – what is the next step? — Order chest X‑ray and sputum microscopy; if positive, start amphotericin B for possible dissemination.
Why is amphotericin B preferred over fluconazole in severe blastomycosis? — Amphotericin B has fungicidal activity and penetrates CNS and bone, whereas fluconazole is less effective.
A patient improves on itraconazole but develops hepatotoxicity – what is the alternative? — Switch to fluconazole if itraconazole is unavailable; monitor liver enzymes.
What clinical feature distinguishes blastomycosis skin lesions from metastatic squamous cell carcinoma? — Broad‑based budding yeast on histology; lesions are often verrucous and may ulcerate.

Why should a clinician suspect blastomycosis in a patient with pulmonary symptoms and a history of travel to the Ohio River valley? — The region is endemic for Blastomyces dermatitidis; inhalation of soil spores is common there.
A patient with disseminated blastomycosis presents with seizures – what is the most likely complication? — CNS involvement (meningitis or brain abscess) due to fungal dissemination.
